A Gordita Ain’t a Pita

by Jim Behymer · August 26, 2026

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:47
Instaread

If you are an American who grew up in small-town Midwest like me and the closest thing you had to Mexican food growing up was Taco Bell (or more dire, Taco Johns), you might be forgiven for having weird ideas about Gorditas. I’d forgive you anyway–I can’t speak for any Mexicans out there. In the late 90s, a time when my go-to item at Taco Bell was the blandly inoffensive chicken soft taco (add sour cream)–mostly because my preferred chilito was no longer available–the exotic-sounding Gordita seemed like an adventurous new thing to try. So when I did, and it turned out to be a pretty normal Taco Bell-style taco that used a pocketless pita as its shell…

Well I’ve always hated the word “underwhelm”–what originally was a fun gag reversal of the actual archaic English word “overwhelm” but has become a dull cliche. But Taco Bell’s Gorditas were underwhelming, limp and colorless, soft and stodgy and generally just too bready for the meager amount of filling they were given. After a few years, Taco Bell phased out this version of their “gordita” in favor of the “cheesy gordita crunch,” ushering in the “5 stoners in a basement mixing up weird shit” phase of Taco Bell’s R&D department. It was around that same time that I started eating, well not real Mexican food but more of the small-town Midwestern version of Mexican food, where they bring a big plate of chips and salsa to your table gratis and every dish is made with tiny bits of steak or huge strips of chicken covered in a layer of that inexplicably addictive white cheese sauce. So I lost track of Taco Bell’s menu for a while. But it turns out the cheesy gordita crunch is still available to this day, and still…forgettable.

But a Gordita ain’t a pita. Gorditas are closer to the Venezuelan-style arepas we wrote about a few years ago. Both have histories stretching back to pre-Columbian times; both are thick cornflour flatbreads, gorditas made from nixtamalized masa harina rather than the non-nistamalized masarepa used for arepas; both served with mostly savory fillings, stewed, shredded meats, cheese, beans, etc. The word “gordita” comes from the Spanish gorda, or fat, and the diminutive suffix –ito, so it’s usually translated as “little fatty” or “little chubby” and is essentially a fat little tortilla that, rather than being wrapped around fillings like the Taco Bell version, is split open and stuffed.

I have never really paid them much attention previously. I see them on the occasional menu but find myself sticking to the usual suspects, the tacos, the burritos, the tostadas, even the huaraches that are less common but that I enjoy so much. I may have ordered one at some point in the past, I have a vague memory of consuming a supermercado taqueria gordita once. But functionally, my first real experience with a Gordita came earlier this month, when I met a bike friend at Gorditas La Tia on 63rd Street in Chicago’s Clearing neighborhood west of Midway Airport.

Between the two of us, we ordered 4 different fillings: refried beans with queso fresco, roasted poblanos with melted cheese, chicharrones in salsa verde, and al pastor pork. Each came in a thin layer inside the gordita, dressed with shredded lettuce and a slice of tomato. The gorditas themselves were thinner than I expected, much thinner than the arepas I’ve had, strong enough to hold their fillings but supple, bendy, like 2 freshly griddled corn tortillas joined along one side.

To be honest, I’m not sure I can do any better than the gorditas I had at La Tia. But I’ll take any excuse to cook some Mexican food. So I started by making refried beans, soaking dried pintos overnight before simmering them with bay leaves and then frying them with onions, garlic, and cumin in lard and smashing them roughly with the back of a spoon.

I also made a Durango-style salsa guajillo, savory and mildly spicy; crisp chicharrones, rewarmed in lard and then braised in salsa verde; a quick shredded chicken tinga, stewed in a smoky, spicy, and savory mix of tomatoes, onions, and chipotle. Along with the beans and various shredded or crumbled cheeses, these would provide plenty of variety for gordita fillings–or for nacho toppings, if I failed miserably to make gorditas.

I have read many a recipe for the gorditas themselves and very few of them agree on the details. The consensue seems to be that the dough should be wet enough so that the edges don’t crack too badly when shaping a small ball of masa into a thick circle using a tortilla press rather than your hands. But the details–some recipes include only masa harina, water, and salt. Others add a leavning agent like baking soda. Some add vegetable oil or lard. Some add wheat flour in addition to the corn flour. The recipes might call for baking the gorditas on a dry griddle-or comal–but they might also call for frying them in oil. All of the recipes give advice on how to get the gorditas to “puff up” so that they are easier to cut open.

I used corn flour, salt, and water only, and coated my cast iron griddle with a little lard before cooking the gorditas. But I did not succeed in getting any of my gorditas to puff up. I had to cut them open carefully with a very sharp knife.

And my gorditas were not as soft, as supple, as thin as those I’d had at Gorditas La Tia. They were thicker, stodgier, more brittle. But these fillings were top-notch, the beans creamy and lush, given textural interest by the crumbles of milky, salty queso fresco and the crunch of pungent onion and livened by the bright cilantro and savory, spicy salsa guajillo. Those fillings would be equally as delicious in another form factor though.

I’m a fan of chicharrones with salsa verde, especially freshly made, when the salsa hasn’t quite soaked all the way through the crisply-fried pork skin, so that the texture still ranges from firm to soft, and it combines well with a mild, buttery queso quesadilla, slowly softening and melting the cheese into stretchy goo. But the ideal vehicle for these to me is the flat, thick, sandal-shaped masa pancake called huarache, which can support any number of condiments in addition to the pork and cheese, onions and cilantro.

Best of all maybe was the chicken tinga, the type of stewed meat guisado that I had read was the ideal filling for a gordita. The chicken pulled apart into soft strands, bound by a chipotle/tomato sauce that comes about as close to an American-style barbecue sauce as Mexican food gets, smoky, spicy, and a little sweet. I white-girl-tacoed this particular filling, topping it with shredded lettuce and diced tomato, with a sprinkling of queso cotija to help bring out the flavors of the tinga, and this particular gordita was probably the best of the ones I made.

These were all good fillings, and would be even better in a competently-made gordita. But they’d be better yet in another format–tacos, burritos, tostadas, huaraches, even tortas! I don’t know that I’ve completely warmed up to gorditas, and when Mexican cuisine offers so many other ways to consume their delicious meats, stews, and spreads, it can be difficult for a new-to-me platform to grab my attention. But I can’t imagine I’m done with the gordita entirely–there are after all plenty of supermercado taquerias out there and I’m bound to order one again sometime.

Jim Behymer
